key_terms.meaning: Describes matter by a few measured bulk properties (p, V, T, m); the basis of engineering thermodynamics.
Matter treated as continuous; ρ = lim δm/δV as δV → δV′. Valid when Kn = λ/L is below about 0.01.
λ = kT/(√2 π d² p); about 67 nm for room air at 101.325 kPa.
Fixed mass; heat and work may cross; boundary may move (control mass).
Mass crosses the control surface; control volume. Mass balance m₂ = m₁ + mᵢ − mₑ.
No mass, no heat, no work crosses.
Independent of mass (p, T); proportional to mass (V, U); extensive per kg (v = V/m).
Two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible system.
pv = RT, pV = mRT, R = R̄/M; air R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K).
Properties: ∮dX = 0. Heat and work: depend on the path, written δQ, δW.
Thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium together; nothing changes, nothing flows.
A chain of equilibrium states; drawn as a line, so W = ∫p dV applies.
Bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
T = 273.16 K × p/pₜₚ at constant volume, in the low-pressure limit; T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15.
Q > 0 into the system, W > 0 done by the system; net energy in = Q − W.
W = ∫p dV; p(V₂ − V₁) at constant p; p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) for pV = C; (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) for pVⁿ = C.
Shaft 2πNτ; electrical VIt; spring ½k(x₂² − x₁²); film σ dA; flow work pV.

takeaways: Engineering thermodynamics uses the macroscopic approach, which rests on the continuum; the continuum holds when the Knudsen number λ/L is far below 0.01, as it is for room air in any ordinary pipe.
Draw the boundary first: whether mass crosses decides closed or open, and the same tank can be either, depending on the boundary.
A property depends only on the state; two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible system, and pv = RT links p, v and T for an ideal gas.
On a state diagram a state is a point, a quasi-static process a line and a cycle a closed loop; every property returns to its first value round a cycle.
Equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance; steady readings with flow mean steady state, not equilibrium.
A quasi-static process passes through equilibrium states, so its work is the area ∫p dV; quasi-static does not mean reversible.
The zeroth law makes temperature a property; thermometers need a thermometric property and fixed points, and the gas thermometer gives a scale independent of the substance.
Heat and work are energy crossing the boundary, not stored in the system; fix the sign convention (Q in positive, W out positive) before any number.
Displacement work depends on the path: from 800 kPa and 0.05 m³ to 0.20 m³ it is 120, 55.45 or 45.37 kJ along p = C, pV = C or pV¹·³ = C.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the classification of systems with sketches, the difference between point and path functions, the zeroth law with temperature scales, and displacement work on standard paths. The newer syllabi also ask for the state postulate, state diagrams and the ideal gas equation of state, so keep a p–v sketch and a worked pv = RT ready.

bank.q: Define system, boundary and surroundings. Classify thermodynamic systems into closed, open and isolated, giving one engineering example of each with a sketch showing what crosses the boundary.
outline: Definitions of system, boundary, surroundings
Closed: fixed mass, heat and work may cross (piston–cylinder)
Open: mass and energy cross (turbine, compressor)
Isolated: nothing crosses (ideal vacuum flask)
Sketches with dashed boundaries and arrows
The boundary, not the hardware, decides the type
answer: System, surroundings, boundary. A system is the quantity of matter or the region of space chosen for study. The surroundings are everything outside it that can interact with it. The boundary is the real or imaginary surface between them; it may be fixed (a tank wall) or moving (a piston face). Mass, heat and work are counted only where they cross the boundary.

Closed system (control mass). No mass crosses the boundary, so the mass inside is constant; heat and work may cross and the boundary may move. Example: gas in a sealed piston–cylinder of an air compressor while both valves are shut. The gas can be heated (Q) and can push the piston (W), but its mass stays the same.

Open system (control volume). Mass crosses the boundary, called the control surface, and carries energy with it; heat and work may also cross. Example: a steam turbine, with steam entering at the inlet, leaving at the exhaust and shaft work leaving through the coupling. Other examples are a compressor, a boiler, a car radiator.

Isolated system. Neither mass nor energy crosses: no mass, Q = 0, W = 0. Example: hot coffee in an ideal sealed vacuum flask, which no real flask achieves exactly. A system together with its surroundings forms an isolated system.

svg.aria: Three sketches with dashed boundaries: a piston-cylinder with heat in and work out but fixed mass; a turbine with mass entering and leaving and shaft work out; an insulated rigid flask with nothing crossing.

answer: Boundary types. A diathermic wall passes heat; an adiabatic wall does not. A rigid wall cannot do boundary work; a movable wall, such as a piston, can. An isolated system needs a boundary that is adiabatic and rigid, with no shaft or wire crossing and no opening.

The boundary decides. The same tank can be either kind: a tank losing air through a valve is open if the boundary is the tank wall and valve, and closed if the boundary wraps only the air that stays inside, a boundary that moves as that air expands.

Check with numbers. A rigid tank holds 2.0 kg of air and 0.50 kg escapes. Around the tank: m₂ = m₁ + mᵢ − mₑ = 2.0 + 0 − 0.50 = 1.5 kg, mass crossed, so open. Around the 1.5 kg that stays: mᵢ = mₑ = 0, so m₂ = m₁ = 1.5 kg, closed. Heat leaves both, so neither is isolated.

bank.q: Compare the microscopic and macroscopic approaches to thermodynamics, with the merits and limits of each. Explain the continuum assumption and show with numbers when it fails.
outline: Microscopic: molecules and statistics
Macroscopic: a few measured properties
Comparison table and which one engineering uses
Continuum: density as a limit over δV′
Knudsen number Kn = λ/L and its rule of thumb
Numbers: Kn for a pipe at 1 atm and in a vacuum
answer: Microscopic approach. Matter is a collection of molecules. Each has a position, a velocity and an energy, and their behaviour is described by statistics: kinetic theory and statistical thermodynamics. Pressure is the average momentum the molecules give a wall per unit area per second; temperature measures their average random kinetic energy.

Macroscopic approach. Matter is treated as a body described by a few quantities that instruments measure: pressure, volume, temperature, mass. No assumption about molecules is needed; the laws come from experiment. This is classical thermodynamics, the approach engineering uses.

head: Point
Microscopic
Macroscopic
rows: the whole body or a small element
about six per molecule, for about 10²⁵ molecules per m³
a few: p, V, T, m
explains what p, T and internal energy are
too many variables for routine work
cannot explain why properties behave as they do

answer: Which engineering uses. Design of engines, boilers, turbines and refrigerators uses the macroscopic approach: an engineer needs heat, work and energy changes, which follow from measured properties. The microscopic view is used to explain them and in special fields.

The continuum assumption. The macroscopic approach treats matter as continuous: density at a point is ρ = lim δm/δV as δV shrinks to a small volume δV′ that still holds very many molecules. Below δV′ the count of molecules in the volume fluctuates by about √N, so δm/δV scatters.

When it fails. The test is the Knudsen number Kn = λ/L, the mean free path over the size of the region. Kn below about 0.01: continuum holds. Kn near 1 or above: it fails, and the microscopic treatment is needed, as in vacuum chambers, the upper atmosphere and micro-channels.

answer.text: Check with numbers for air at 300 K, taking d = 3.7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m:

answer: Conclusion. Both approaches describe the same state and agree. The macroscopic approach, resting on the continuum, is valid for ordinary engineering equipment because Kn there is tiny, as the pipe shows.

bank.q: Define property, state, path, process and cycle, and distinguish intensive, extensive and specific properties. State the state postulate for a simple compressible substance, give the ideal gas equation of state, and show processes on a state diagram.
outline: Property and the path-independence test
Intensive, extensive and specific, with a halving test
State and state point
State postulate: two independent intensive properties
pv = RT with R = R̄/M
Processes as lines on a p–v diagram
Cycle: zero net property change
answer: Property. A characteristic of a system that has a definite value in a given state and does not depend on how the state was reached: p, T, V, U, ρ. Test: its change between two states is the same on every path, and its change round a cycle is zero.

Intensive, extensive, specific. Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter (p, T, ρ); extensive properties are proportional to it (m, V, U, H); a specific property is an extensive property per unit mass (v = V/m, u = U/m), and behaves as intensive.

answer.text: Halving test with numbers. 2.0 kg of air at 100 kPa and 300 K has V = mRT/p = 2.0 × 0.287 × 300 ÷ 100 = 1.722 m³. Split it into two equal parts:

answer: State and state point. The state is the condition of the system described by the values of its properties at one instant, when it is in equilibrium. Drawn on a diagram of two properties, it is a state point.

State postulate. The state of a simple compressible system, one where volume change is the only important work mode, is fixed by two independent intensive properties. In a single phase p and T are independent; during boiling they are not, so p with v (or dryness fraction) is used.
Equation of state. It links p, v and T. For an ideal gas pv = RT with R = R̄/M; for air R = 8.314 ÷ 28.97 = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Knowing any two of p, v, T gives the third.

answer.text: State diagrams. A state is a point on a p–v, T–v or p–T diagram; a quasi-static process is a line; a cycle is a closed loop. Constant-volume, constant-pressure and isothermal lines through one state of air:

svg.aria: A p–v diagram for air with state point 1 at 0.861 cubic metres per kilogram and 100 kPa, a vertical constant-volume line, a horizontal constant-pressure line and the 300 K isotherm through it.

answer: Path, process, cycle. A process is a change from one state to another; the path is the series of states it passes through. A cycle is a series of processes ending in the starting state, so every property change over a cycle is zero. Processes are named by what is held constant: isochoric, isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic.

answer.text: Check with numbers. State 1 above, 100 kPa and 300 K:
answer.pre:
v₁ = RT/p = 0.287 × 300 / 100 = 0.861 m³/kg
keep v, double p to 200 kPa:  T = pv/R = 200 × 0.861 / 0.287 = 600 K
keep p, double v to 1.722:    T = 100 × 1.722 / 0.287 = 600 K
two different paths, same end temperature 600 K: T is a property

bank.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it leads to the concept of temperature and the use of thermometers. Describe how temperature scales are set up, including the ideal-gas and thermodynamic temperature scales.
outline: Exact statement with three bodies
Temperature as the property equal in thermal equilibrium
Thermometer as the third body
Thermometric property and two fixed points
Gas thermometer and the triple point of water, 273.16 K
Thermodynamic scale and the kelvin
Numerical check
answer: Statement. When two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Thermal equilibrium means that, in contact through a diathermic wall, neither body changes any more.

Temperature as a property. The law makes thermal equilibrium shared. All bodies in equilibrium with a given reference body can be given one label, and bodies with equal labels show no change when they touch. That label is temperature: the property that is equal for bodies in thermal equilibrium.

The thermometer. The third body is the thermometer. Placed in body A until its reading stops changing, it is in equilibrium with A; placed in B, likewise. Equal readings mean A and B are at the same temperature without ever touching. Unequal readings tell which way heat would flow on contact: from the higher reading to the lower.

Thermometric property and fixed points. A thermometer needs a property X that changes steadily with temperature: liquid length, gas pressure at constant volume, resistance, thermocouple emf. A linear two-point scale fixes it at the ice point (0 °C) and steam point (100 °C): t = 100 (X − Xᵢ)/(Xₛ − Xᵢ). Different properties agree at the fixed points but not exactly in between.

Single fixed point and the ideal-gas scale. A constant-volume gas thermometer is referred to the triple point of water, 273.16 K: T = 273.16 K × p/pₜₚ, taken in the limit of very little gas. In that limit all gases agree, so the scale does not depend on the substance.

Thermodynamic temperature scale. The second law defines a temperature from the heat ratio of a reversible engine, Q₁/Q₂ = T₁/T₂, with no substance at all. It coincides with the ideal-gas scale. Since 2019 the kelvin is fixed by the Boltzmann constant, 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K exactly. Celsius is the same scale shifted: T = t + 273.15.

answer.pre:
gas thermometer: pₜₚ = 60.00 kPa, p = 75.00 kPa
T = 273.16 × 75.00 / 60.00 = 341.45 K,  t = 341.45 − 273.15 = 68.30 °C
thermocouple e = 0.20t − 0.0005t² mV, meter linear through 0 and 100 °C:
e(100) = 15 mV, e(50) = 8.75 mV  →  meter shows 100 × 8.75/15 = 58.33 °C
the two scales agree at 0 and 100 °C only

answer: Conclusion. The zeroth law gives equality of temperature; thermometric properties and fixed points give numbers; the gas thermometer and the second law give a scale independent of any substance.

bank.q: A gas in a piston–cylinder expands from V₁ = 0.10 m³ to V₂ = 0.30 m³, starting at p₁ = 200 kPa. Find the displacement work and the final pressure if the path is (a) constant pressure, (b) pV = constant, (c) pV¹·⁴ = constant. Show the paths on a p–V diagram and comment.
outline: W = ∫p dV for each path
p–V sketch of the three paths
Same end volume, different work: work is a path function
answer: Method. For a quasi-static process the work done by the gas is W = ∫p dV from V₁ to V₂, the area under the path on a p–V diagram. With p in kPa and V in m³, W is in kJ.

Formulas from the integral. Constant p: p comes out of the integral, W = p(V₂ − V₁). pV = C: p = C/V, so W = C ∫dV/V = C ln(V₂/V₁) with C = p₁V₁. pVⁿ = C (n ≠ 1): W = C ∫V⁻ⁿ dV = C (V₂¹⁻ⁿ − V₁¹⁻ⁿ)/(1 − n); since C V₂¹⁻ⁿ = p₂V₂ and C V₁¹⁻ⁿ = p₁V₁, this is (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1).
(a) Constant pressure. W = p(V₂ − V₁) = 200 × (0.30 − 0.10) = 200 × 0.20 = 40.0 kJ. Final pressure 200 kPa.

answer.text: p–V diagram. The three paths from the same state 1 to the same final volume:

svg.aria: A p–V diagram from state 1 at 200 kPa and 0.10 cubic metres to 0.30 cubic metres along three paths: constant pressure, pV constant ending at 66.67 kPa, and pV to the 1.4 constant ending at 42.96 kPa.

answer: Comment. The start state and final volume are the same, but the work differs: the faster the pressure falls during expansion, the lower the curve and the smaller the area under it. Work is a path function. All three are positive because the gas expands and does work on the piston.

Order of the answers. The exponent n in pVⁿ = C sets how steeply p falls: n = 0 (constant pressure) gives the largest work, n = 1 less, n = 1.4 less still, and n → ∞ (constant volume) gives zero. For an ideal gas, n = 1 is isothermal and n = γ ≈ 1.4 is a slow adiabatic expansion, so (c) is close to an expansion with no heat supplied.
Check. For (b), a crude sum with two strips at the midpoints V = 0.15 and 0.25 m³ gives (133.3 + 80.0) × 0.10 = 21.3 kJ, close to 21.97 kJ, so the logarithm is in the right range.

bank.q: A gas in a cylinder is compressed with 40 kJ of work input while 25 kJ of heat leaves it. Fix a sign convention, write W and Q with signs and find the change in the energy of the gas. Repeat in the other common convention.
outline: Convention: Q positive in, W positive out
W = −40 kJ, Q = −25 kJ
ΔE = Q − W = +15 kJ
Other convention: W′ = +40 kJ, ΔE = Q + W′ = +15 kJ
Same physics either way
answer: Convention. Heat into the system is positive (Q > 0); work done by the system on the surroundings is positive (W > 0). Heat leaving and work done on the system are negative.
Signs. 40 kJ of work is done on the gas during compression: W = −40 kJ. 25 kJ of heat leaves the gas: Q = −25 kJ.

Net energy change. The energy received by the gas through heat and work is Q − W = (−25) − (−40) = +15 kJ. With no other energy crossing, the energy stored in the gas, its internal energy, rises by 15 kJ (this is the first law for a closed system, ΔE = Q − W).
Physical meaning. The piston pushed 40 kJ in; 25 kJ leaked out as heat because the compressed gas became hotter than the cylinder wall; 15 kJ stays in the gas, which ends hotter than it started.

The other convention. Some books count work done on the system as positive and write ΔE = Q + W′. Then W′ = +40 kJ, Q = −25 kJ, and ΔE = −25 + 40 = +15 kJ. The numbers on the page change sign; the physics, a 15 kJ rise, does not.

Why the gas got hotter. For an ideal gas the internal energy depends on temperature only, so a 15 kJ rise in internal energy means a rise in temperature. Had the cylinder been perfectly lagged (adiabatic), all 40 kJ would have stayed in the gas and the temperature rise would have been larger.

Where the boundary sits. The boundary is the gas; the piston face is part of it. The work input crosses at the moving piston face, and the heat crosses at the cylinder wall. Choosing the gas plus the cylinder metal as the system would change the heat figure (some energy would be stored in the warmed metal) but not the method.
Exam habit. Write the convention in the first line, turn each phrase ('rejected', 'supplied', 'done on', 'done by') into a signed number, then substitute. Never change the convention part way.
Check. If the gas had been compressed with no heat loss (adiabatic), ΔE would be +40 kJ; if all 40 kJ had leaked away as heat, ΔE would be 0. The answer +15 kJ lies between these limits, as it must.

bank.q: A rigid tank of gas is stirred by a paddle driven with a torque of 12 N·m at 300 rpm for 5 minutes, while a heater inside the tank draws 2.0 A at 230 V for the same time. Find the shaft work, the electrical work and the total work with signs. Then find the work to stretch a soap film (σ = 0.025 N/m) on a frame 50 mm wide by 20 mm, and the work to stretch a spring (k = 400 N/m) from 0.10 m to 0.20 m. Show the force–displacement pattern in each.
outline: Shaft: W = 2πNτ = 113.1 kJ on the gas
Electrical: W = VIt = 138.0 kJ on the gas
Total W = −251.1 kJ in this book's convention
Soap film: two surfaces, W = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ J
Spring: ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = 6.0 J
Generalised force × displacement table
answer: Pattern. Every work mode is a generalised force times the change of its paired displacement: pressure and volume, torque and angle, voltage and charge, tension and length, surface tension and area.

Shaft (paddle) work. N = 300 rev/min × 5 min = 1500 rev. W = 2πNτ = 2π × 1500 × 12 = 113 097 J = 113.1 kJ, done on the gas. Power = 2πnτ/60 = 2π × 300 × 12 ÷ 60 = 377 W; check 377 W × 300 s = 113.1 kJ.
Electrical work. W = VIt = 230 × 2.0 × 300 = 138 000 J = 138.0 kJ, done on the gas (the heater is inside the boundary, so this is work, not heat).
Total work, with signs. Both are done on the system, so in this book's convention W = −113.1 − 138.0 = −251.1 kJ. The tank is rigid, so displacement work is zero.

Surface-tension work. A soap film on a wire frame 50 mm wide is stretched by moving the slider 20 mm. The film has two surfaces, so dA = 2 × 0.050 × 0.020 = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m². W = σ dA = 0.025 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 5.0 × 10⁻⁵ J, done on the film.
Spring work. For a linear spring, F = kx and W = ∫kx dx = ½k(x₂² − x₁²). With k = 400 N/m from 0.10 to 0.20 m: W = 200 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 6.0 J.
Note. Stirring work can only enter a fluid: a paddle cannot take shaft work back out of a stirred gas. The 251.1 kJ raises the gas's internal energy, minus any heat that leaks out.
Check. Electrical work = voltage × charge = 230 V × 600 C = 138 000 J, the same as VIt; shaft work = torque × angle = 12 × 9424.8 rad = 113 097 J.

bank.q: A constant-volume gas thermometer reads 100.0 kPa at the ice point and 136.6 kPa at the steam point. Find the temperature when the pressure is 118.0 kPa, on a linear scale. State the thermometric property, check the answer with the ideal-gas relation, and explain why gas thermometers are extrapolated to zero pressure.
outline: Thermometric property: pressure at constant volume
Ratio 1.366 shows near-ideal behaviour
Extrapolation to zero pressure gives the ideal-gas scale
answer: Thermometric property. The pressure of a fixed mass of gas held at constant volume. It rises steadily with temperature, which makes it a good thermometric property.

The instrument. A glass or metal bulb holds a fixed mass of gas (often hydrogen, helium or nitrogen) and is joined by a thin tube to a mercury manometer. Before each reading the mercury reservoir is raised or lowered until the mercury touches a fixed mark, so the gas volume is the same at every reading; the manometer then gives the gas pressure.
Linear two-point scale. Assume t = a p + b and fix a and b with the ice point (p = 100.0 kPa at 0 °C) and the steam point (p = 136.6 kPa at 100 °C): t = 100 × (p − pᵢ)/(pₛ − pᵢ).
One-fixed-point check. For an ideal gas at constant volume p ∝ T, so T = Tᵢ × p/pᵢ = 273.15 × 118.0 ÷ 100.0 = 322.32 K. The two methods agree to 0.01 K.

Is the gas nearly ideal? For an ideal gas the steam-to-ice pressure ratio should be 373.15 ÷ 273.15 = 1.3661. Here 136.6 ÷ 100.0 = 1.366, the same to four figures, so this thermometer behaves ideally over the range.

Sensitivity. The pressure rises by 36.6 kPa over 100 °C, so 0.366 kPa per °C. A reading error of 0.1 kPa would shift the result by 0.1 ÷ 0.366 = 0.27 °C, which is why the volume is reset to the mark before each reading.

Ideal-gas scale. Real gases deviate a little from p ∝ T, more at high pressure. Readings are therefore taken with less and less gas in the bulb and extrapolated to zero pressure; in that limit every gas gives the same temperature, the ideal-gas temperature, equal to the thermodynamic temperature. The modern reference point is the triple point of water, 273.16 K, with T = 273.16 K × p/pₜₚ.

bank.q: A frictionless piston of mass 30 kg and diameter 80 mm holds 0.500 litre of air in a vertical cylinder; the atmosphere is at 100 kPa. Find the air pressure. 10 kg of sand is then added grain by grain, the air staying at room temperature. Find the final pressure and volume, the piston drop and the work, and explain why the process is quasi-static.
outline: Force balance including the atmosphere: p₁ = 158.55 kPa
p₂ = 178.07 kPa
pV = C: V₂ = 0.4452 L, drop 10.9 mm
W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = −9.20 J
Each grain gives a new equilibrium state, so a line on p–V
Sudden loading would reach the same state by a different route
answer: Forces on the piston. Up: the air pressure on the piston face, pA. Down: the atmosphere on the top face, pₐₜₘA, and the weight of the piston and anything on it, (m + mₛ)g. With no friction and the piston at rest, the two balance: pA = pₐₜₘA + (m + mₛ)g. Mechanical equilibrium fixes the air pressure; the volume then follows from the temperature.
Piston area. A = πD²/4 = π × 0.080² ÷ 4 = 5.027 × 10⁻³ m².
Equilibrium with the piston only. Forces on the piston at rest: pA = pₐₜₘA + mg, so p₁ = pₐₜₘ + mg/A = 100 + 30 × 9.81 ÷ (5.027 × 10⁻³ × 1000) = 100 + 58.55 = 158.55 kPa.
Final volume. Sand is added grain by grain and the air stays at room temperature, so the process is quasi-static with pV constant: V₂ = V₁ p₁/p₂ = 0.500 × 158.55 ÷ 178.07 = 0.4452 L.
Work. Along pV = C: W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 158.55 kPa × 0.500 × 10⁻³ m³ × ln(0.8904) = 79.27 J × (−0.11612) = −9.20 J: 9.20 J of work is done on the air.

Why quasi-static matters. Every intermediate state has one pressure, so the path is the curve pV = 79.27 J and the area under it is the work. If the 10 kg were dropped at once, the end state would be the same after the motion died out and the air cooled, but the in-between states would have no single pressure; the work done on the air would then be pₑₓₜ|ΔV| = 178.07 × 5.48 × 10⁻⁵ kJ = 9.76 J, not 9.20 J.

Area check. A straight line from (0.500 L, 158.55 kPa) to (0.4452 L, 178.07 kPa) has area ½ × (158.55 + 178.07) × 0.0548 × 10⁻³ kJ = 9.22 J, just above the curved-path value 9.20 J, because the curve sags slightly below the straight chord.
Check. p₂V₂ = 178.07 × 0.4452 = 79.28 J ≈ p₁V₁ = 79.27 J, as the isothermal path requires.

bank.q: Two copper blocks, 2.0 kg at 400 K and 3.0 kg at 300 K (c = 0.385 kJ/(kg·K)), are enclosed together in insulation. Describe what happens when they are separated by (a) a diathermic wall and (b) an adiabatic wall. Find the final temperature and the heat transferred in (a), and relate the result to the zeroth law.
outline: Diathermic: heat flows hot to cold until temperatures equal
Energy balance gives T = 340 K
Q = 46.2 kJ, checked from both blocks
Thermal equilibrium; zeroth law and a thermometer
Adiabatic: no heat flow, 400 K and 300 K stay
answer: Diathermic wall. It lets heat pass. The 400 K block is hotter, so heat flows from it to the 300 K block until both reach one temperature. The hotter block cools and the colder one warms.

Final temperature. The pair is enclosed by insulation and does no work, so the heat lost by the hot block equals the heat gained by the cold one: m₁c(T₁ − T) = m₂c(T − T₂). Same material, so c cancels: 2.0 × (400 − T) = 3.0 × (T − 300).
Heat transferred. Q = m₁c(T₁ − T) = 2.0 × 0.385 × (400 − 340) = 46.2 kJ from the hot block to the cold block. Check: m₂c(T − T₂) = 3.0 × 0.385 × (340 − 300) = 46.2 kJ.

Energy check for the pair. The two blocks inside the insulation form an isolated system: no heat or work crosses the outer boundary. The hot block's internal energy falls by 46.2 kJ and the cold block's rises by 46.2 kJ, so the total is unchanged, as it must be.
Name of the final condition. Both blocks at 340 K: thermal equilibrium. By the zeroth law, a thermometer that reads 340 K (66.85 °C) in one block reads the same in the other.
Process for the hotter block. It loses heat at nearly constant volume (a solid), so its process is a cooling at constant volume; for the hot block taken as the system, Q = −46.2 kJ and W ≈ 0.

Why the final temperature is nearer 300 K. The cold block has more mass (3.0 kg against 2.0 kg) and the same specific heat, so it takes a larger heat capacity to warm; the common temperature is the mass-weighted average, (2.0 × 400 + 3.0 × 300) ÷ 5.0 = 340 K.

Adiabatic wall. No heat crosses, so each block keeps its temperature: 400 K and 300 K indefinitely. They are not in thermal equilibrium with each other, yet nothing changes; an adiabatic wall makes them two separate systems, and the zeroth law says nothing about them.

bank.q: Air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) at 150 kPa, 0.10 m³ and 300 K is taken round the cycle: heating at constant volume to 300 kPa, expansion at constant pressure to 0.25 m³, cooling at constant volume to 150 kPa, and compression at constant pressure back to the start. Using this cycle, show that temperature and volume are point functions while work and heat are path functions.
outline: Point and path functions defined; exact and inexact differentials
Mass 0.1742 kg; temperatures 300, 600, 1500, 750 K
ΔT and ΔV sum to zero round the cycle
Net work = enclosed area = 22.5 kJ
Two paths 1→3 give 45.0 and 22.5 kJ
∮δQ = ∮δW = 22.5 kJ
answer: Point and path functions. A property (point function) has one value at each state, so its change between two states does not depend on the path, and ∮dX = 0 round any cycle. Heat and work (path functions) exist only while crossing the boundary; their amounts depend on the path, and their small amounts δQ, δW are inexact differentials.

Properties close; work does not. ΔT and ΔV sum to zero round the cycle, as for any property. The work sums to +22.5 kJ, the area of the rectangle (150 kPa × 0.15 m³), positive because the loop runs clockwise on p–V.

Two paths, same end states. From 1 to 3: via 2, W = 0 + 45.0 = 45.0 kJ; via 4, W = 150 × 0.15 + 0 = 22.5 kJ. Both give ΔT = 1200 K and ΔV = 0.15 m³. Same property changes, different work: work is a path function.

Heat. For a cycle the first law gives ∮δQ = ∮δW, so the net heat received is also +22.5 kJ, not zero. Heat is a path function too: along each path from 1 to 3, Q = ΔU + W, with the same ΔU but different W, so Q differs by 45.0 − 22.5 = 22.5 kJ.

Exact and inexact differentials. For a property X, ∫dX from 1 to 3 = X₃ − X₁ whatever the path, so dX is exact. For work, ∫δW from 1 to 3 is 45.0 kJ on one path and 22.5 kJ on the other; there is no function 'W' with W₃ − W₁ equal to both, so δW is inexact, and we write W₁₃, never ΔW.
Conclusion. A cycle returns every property to its first value, but the net work and net heat equal the enclosed area, here 22.5 kJ. That is exactly what lets an engine deliver work cycle after cycle.

bank.q: Contrast a quasi-static process with a real rapid process in an engine cylinder. Evaluate, with numbers, the error made by using W = ∫p dV for a rapid process, and state when the quasi-static assumption is acceptable.
outline: Quasi-static: equilibrium states, a line on p–V
Rapid: no single pressure; use the pressure at the piston face
Numbers: 28.58 J slow against 31.23 J sudden, error 9.3 %
Free expansion: W = 0
Acceptable when the process is slow compared with pressure equalisation (about 0.3 ms against a 10 ms stroke)
answer: Quasi-static process. Infinitely slow: the system passes through equilibrium states, with one pressure and one temperature at every instant, so the path is a line on p–V and W = ∫p dV is the area under it.

Real rapid process. In an engine cylinder at high speed, the gas near the piston is at a different pressure from the gas at the head, the charge swirls, and the piston may overshoot. These states have no single p, so ∫p dV along 'the' path has no meaning. The work actually done on the piston is ∫pₚ dV, where pₚ is the pressure on the piston face; for expansion against a constant outside pressure it is pₑₓₜ ΔV.

answer.text: Size of the error, with numbers. A piston (D = 100 mm, 50 kg) holds 1.000 L of air at 163.78 kPa with the atmosphere at 101.325 kPa. 25 kg of sand is added, and the air ends at 195.00 kPa and 0.8399 L at room temperature, by two routes:

answer: Evaluate. Using ∫p dV for the sudden process would give 28.58 J, but 31.23 J was really supplied: an error of (31.23 − 28.58) ÷ 28.58 = 9.3 %. The extra 2.65 J was dissipated in the piston's bouncing and in eddies, and left as extra heat to the room.
Free expansion: the extreme case. Gas expanding into a vacuum does no work at all, W = 0, while ∫p dV along any assumed path would give a positive number. The error is then 100 %.

When the assumption is acceptable. When the process is slow compared with the time the gas needs to even out its pressure. That time is roughly the cylinder length divided by the speed of sound: 0.1 m ÷ 340 m/s ≈ 0.3 ms. An engine stroke at 3000 rpm takes 10 ms, about 30 times longer, so ideal cycle analysis is a fair first estimate; very fast processes such as a burst diaphragm are not.
Practice. Engineers compute quasi-static work, then correct with measured efficiencies, or measure real indicator diagrams with fast pressure sensors and take their enclosed area.

Conclusion. W = ∫p dV is exact only for quasi-static processes; for rapid ones use the pressure at the moving boundary, pₑₓₜ ΔV for a constant outside pressure, and expect the real work input to exceed the quasi-static value in compression (here by 9.3 %).

bank.q: Distinguish thermodynamic equilibrium from steady state using a steam turbine as the example. Explain why a steady-flow device can still be analysed with equilibrium property tables.
outline: Equilibrium: thermal, mechanical, chemical; no change, no flow
Steady state: constant at each point, with flow and gradients
Turbine: steady but not in equilibrium
Comparison table
Local equilibrium at inlet and outlet allows tables
Balance written between inlet and outlet
answer: Thermodynamic equilibrium. No unbalanced driving force inside the system or between it and its surroundings: thermal (one temperature), mechanical (no unbalanced force, uniform pressure) and chemical (no reaction or diffusion). Nothing changes with time and nothing flows.

Steady state. At each fixed point inside the system the properties do not change with time, but mass and energy flow through and the properties differ from point to point. It is a balance of flows, not an absence of them.

Example: a steam turbine at full load. Steam enters at 500 °C and leaves at 60 °C; each gauge holds its reading for hours. The readings are steady, so the turbine is in steady state. But steam crosses the boundary all the time and there is a 440 °C temperature difference inside, so thermal and mechanical equilibrium both fail: it is not in equilibrium.

head: Equilibrium
Steady state
rows: gas in a closed tank, settled

answer: Why equilibrium tables still work. The steam at the inlet pipe is close to uniform over a small region: a small element of it is nearly in equilibrium even though the turbine as a whole is not. This local equilibrium assumption lets us read h, s and v from steam tables at the inlet and outlet sections.

What the analysis then does. The energy balance is written between inlet and outlet only, without asking about the states inside, and with the mass inside constant (steady state), mass in equals mass out: ṁ₁ = ṁ₂.

Which equilibrium fails in the turbine. Thermal: temperature falls from 500 °C to 60 °C along the flow. Mechanical: pressure falls from inlet to exhaust, and that unbalanced pressure is what drives the steam and turns the blades. Chemical: steam stays steam (some condenses near the exhaust, a phase change in progress). Two of the three fail, so the turbine is far from equilibrium even though it is perfectly steady.

Check with numbers. A closed rigid tank of air at 500 kPa is left in a room at 30 °C. At first the air is hotter than the room and cools; heat flows, so it is not in equilibrium. After some hours the air is at 30 °C, its pressure has fallen to a steady value and no heat flows: equilibrium. Had it been the turbine, steady readings would never have meant equilibrium, because flow never stops.
Conclusion. Constant readings are necessary but not sufficient for equilibrium. Ask whether anything crosses the boundary or whether gradients remain; if so, the system is at most in steady state.

glossary.def: The science of energy, its transfer as heat and work, and the properties of the matter involved.
A description of matter through its molecules and their statistics.
A description of matter through a few measured bulk properties such as p, V and T.
The model of matter as continuous, so that properties have a value at every point.
Kn = λ/L, the mean free path divided by the size of the region; small values mean the continuum holds.
The average distance a molecule travels between collisions.
The matter or region chosen for study.
Everything outside the system that can interact with it.
The real or imaginary surface, fixed or moving, separating a system from its surroundings.
A region in space across whose boundary mass can flow; an open system.
A fixed quantity of matter; a closed system.
A quantity with a definite value in each state, independent of the path.
Two independent intensive properties fix the state of a simple compressible system.
A relation between p, v and T, such as pv = RT for an ideal gas.
A graph of two properties on which each state is a point, such as a p–v diagram.
A change of a system from one state to another.
The series of states a system passes through during a process.
A series of processes that returns the system to its first state.
A quantity whose change depends only on the end states; a property.
A quantity, such as heat or work, whose amount depends on the path.
Thermal, mechanical and chemical equilibrium at once, so that no property changes with time.
A condition in which properties at each point stay constant in time while mass and energy flow through.
A process slow enough that the system passes through a continuous chain of equilibrium states.
Two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
A property that changes steadily with temperature and is used to measure it.
The state where ice, liquid water and vapour coexist, at 273.16 K (0.01 °C).
Energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference.
Energy crossing a boundary whose sole effect outside could be the raising of a weight.
Work done by a moving boundary, W = ∫p dV for a quasi-static process.
The work pV needed to push fluid across a control surface.
